summary: This informational memo describes UTF-7, a way of writing Unicode text using only 7-bit ASCII characters, so it can pass through mail systems that handle only ASCII. It also explains its use within MIME.

eli5.summary: Writing in a fancy alphabet using only the keys on a basic typewriter.

questions: why use utf-7 instead of utf-8 in email
what does the plus sign mean in utf-7
subtitle: A way to write any Unicode text using only 7-bit ASCII, so it survives old mail systems.

tldr.problem: Internet mail carries only 7-bit US-ASCII, but Unicode covers most of the world's writing systems. UTF-8 sends non-ASCII characters as octets above 127, which mail must then encode a second time, bloating non-English text.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-7 writes plain ASCII characters as themselves and wraps everything else in a shifted run: a plus sign, the 16-bit Unicode values in a modified Base64, and an optional minus sign to end the run.
tldr.outcome: The result is mail-safe, readable where the text is mostly ASCII, and compact for other scripts. The RFC says it should be used only on 7-bit transports such as mail, and that UTF-8 or plain Unicode is preferred elsewhere.

facts.label: Average cost outside ASCII
facts.value: 2 2/3 octets per character plus shift octets

today: RFC 2152 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1642. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo itself says it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Mail Needed Another Encoding
sections.content:
Unicode covers most of the world's writing systems, but Internet mail (RFC 822) supports only 7-bit US-ASCII. MIME extends mail to other character sets and lets new ones be registered, but it does not name Unicode as a permitted character set or say how to encode it.

UTF-8 is an obvious candidate, but it uses octets from 128 through 255 for characters outside US-ASCII. In mail those octets must be encoded a second time, so the text goes through two encodings. The RFC notes that UTF-8 with the MIME Quoted-Printable encoding writes US-ASCII characters in one octet but other characters may need up to nine octets. That puts non-English speakers at a disadvantage.

UTF-7 is the proposed fix. It also copes with mail gateways, such as EBCDIC-based ones, that cannot handle all of US-ASCII.
sections.eli5: Old mail pipes only understand a small set of letters. Sending other alphabets through them the long way makes the message much longer, so UTF-7 finds a shorter way.

sections.title: The Three Encoding Rules
sections.content:
The RFC defines three character sets. Set D holds letters, digits and nine marks: ' ( ) , . / : ? and the hyphen. Set O holds optional direct characters such as ! " # $ % & *. Set B is the Base64 alphabet from RFC 2045 without the pad character =.

  • Rule 1: characters in Set D may be written as themselves. Set O characters may also be, but many are illegal in header fields or may not pass some gateways.
  • Rule 2: any Unicode text can be written as a run of Set B characters after the shift character + (decimal 43). The run ends at the first character outside Set B. If that character is a hyphen it is absorbed; any other is processed normally.
  • Rule 3: space, tab, carriage return and line feed may be written directly, subject to MIME's own rules for them.

A literal plus sign is written +-. A + followed by something other than a Set B character or a hyphen is ill-formed. If the first character after a shifted run is itself a hyphen, an extra hyphen is needed so the real one is not absorbed.
sections.eli5: Ordinary letters go through as they are. For anything fancy you write a plus sign, then a scrambled spelling, then a minus sign to say the scramble is over.

sections.title: How a Shifted Run Is Built
sections.content:
Inside a shifted run, each Unicode character is a 16-bit quantity, sent most significant octet first. Surrogate pairs from UTF-16 get no special treatment: each half is simply a separate 16-bit quantity. Characters outside the range reachable through surrogate pairs cannot be encoded, and text with an odd number of octets is ill-formed.

The octet stream is then Base64-encoded as in RFC 2045, except that the = pad is omitted. The pad is left out because = is the escape character of the Q encoding used in header fields by RFC 2047. When encoding, zero bits pad out to a Base64 character boundary. When decoding, leftover bits that do not make a complete 16-bit character are discarded, and if any of them is non-zero the sequence is ill-formed.

Characters covered by Rules 1 and 3 cost one octet each. Other characters average 2 2/3 octets, plus one octet to switch into Base64 and an optional one to switch out.
sections.eli5: Each fancy letter is turned into a number, and the numbers are spelled using only safe letters. Extra bits are filled with zeros, like padding a box with paper.

sections.title: Examples and Use Within MIME
sections.content:
The RFC gives these encodings. The Unicode sequence A, NOT IDENTICAL TO, ALPHA, . becomes A+ImIDkQ.. The Japanese word for Japanese, three Han characters, becomes +ZeVnLIqe-. Hi Mom -, WHITE SMILING FACE, -! becomes Hi Mom -+Jjo--!.

In MIME the character set tag is UTF-7, standing for any Unicode version 2.0 or later. UTF-7 is safe for mail, so it can be used with any content transfer encoding except where line length and line break rules are violated. The 7-bit encoding for bodies and the Q encoding for headers are both acceptable.

A shifted sequence may not cross a line break, so UTF-7 encoding should take place after line breaking. If a line is too long once encoded, a transfer encoding such as Quoted-Printable can be used, or line breaking and UTF-7 encoding can be done together.
sections.eli5: Mail programs just label the message as UTF-7 so the reader knows to unscramble the plus-and-minus parts. Never cut a scrambled part in half across two lines.

sections.title: Why Not UTF-8, and Other Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC compares average octets per character. UTF-8 in Quoted-Printable is judged not viable because of its large expansion for everything except Western European text. UTF-8 in Base64 expands text for non-Western-European users and cannot be read directly even when the content is mostly US-ASCII. UTF-7 gives results competitive with ISO-8859-x while reaching all of Unicode.

The authors also consider mixing character sets with MIME's multipart/mixed. They reject it as a general answer: it does not work in header fields, and it handles occasional symbols or short snippets of other scripts poorly.

The summary says UTF-7 is most effective for text with long runs of US-ASCII mixed with single characters or short strings of Unicode. It should be used only with 7-bit transports such as mail.
sections.eli5: The authors measured how long messages get with each method. UTF-7 stays short for mostly plain text, and you can still read the plain parts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Treat that as an absence of analysis, not a statement that the format is free of risk.

The only related guidance in the text concerns well-formedness: sequences with an odd number of octets, non-zero discarded bits, or a + followed by an invalid character are called ill-formed.
sections.eli5: The authors did not write down any safety rules, so the memo does not tell us anything about safety.
